screens.title: Advanced UI Concepts & Input Handling
screens.subtitle: Control how input moves between game and UI, manage focus for keyboard and gamepad, and build performant interactive screens

narration.text: In this chapter we’ll learn how to manage input and build advanced user interfaces in Unreal Engine 5. You will understand the three input modes the engine provides, how to make menus and inventory screens that won’t let the player accidentally move the character, and how to give UI elements focus for keyboard and gamepad navigation. We’ll also cover using widget animations for polish and practical performance techniques that prevent UI from becoming a runtime bottleneck. For example, when you open a pause menu you’ll need to pause gameplay, show the mouse cursor, and set input so the UI receives events instead of the character. A common mistake is leaving game input active when a menu is open, which can let the player keep moving while the menu is visible. By the end of this lesson you’ll be able to choose the correct input mode, explicitly set focus for controllers, and structure widgets so animations and visibility changes are efficient. Think about a simple pause key: toggling a single function should pause the game, show the menu, change input mode, and play a fade animation. That single flow is the practical goal for your UI work here.

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: Correct input modes and explicit focus are the foundation for reliable, controller-friendly game UIs.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: These four objectives give you a clear skill set to build and manage advanced UIs. First, you will implement robust input handling by choosing between game-only, UI-only, and combined input modes and toggling the mouse cursor appropriately. A practical example is pausing a game and ensuring movement input stops while menu navigation works. Second, you will manage UI navigation and focus for keyboard and gamepad users, using functions that set user focus or keyboard focus and explicit navigation rules when automatic navigation misbehaves. Third, you will design and implement common patterns such as pause menus, inventory screens, and pop-up dialogs, understanding when to create overlays, when to pause the world, and when to change input mode. Finally, you will add widget animation and optimize UI performance: bind animations to C++ properties, play them at construct time, avoid heavy Event Tick usage, and choose the right visibility states to balance responsiveness and memory. Each objective mixes a definition, a concrete application, and a common pitfall to watch for so you can build reliable, accessible interfaces.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Details & Mnemonics
screens.subtitle: Practical steps and quick memory aids for each objective

narration.text: Let’s add practical detail to each objective so you can remember the workflow under pressure. For input modes, use the mnemonic: Game, UI, Both. When opening a full-screen menu choose UIOnly and show the cursor. When you need limited UI touches during play, consider GameAndUI but plan to consume events that should not reach gameplay. For focus and navigation, think: initialize, focus, and lock. Always set the first button to receive focus when a menu opens, and use explicit navigation rules when automatic navigation skips items. For patterns such as pause menus or inventories, follow a small lifecycle: create or show the widget, set input mode, set focus, play entry animation. For animation and performance, remember: bind animation properties in C++ only when you need direct control, avoid Event Tick, and toggle visibility states rather than repeatedly creating widgets when you will reuse them. These micro-checks map directly to common mistakes you’ll encounter during testing.

screens.title: Input Modes Defined
screens.subtitle: What GameOnly, UIOnly, and GameAndUI actually do

narration.text: Input modes determine the destination of player input events. GameOnly routes all keyboard, mouse, and gamepad input to gameplay systems and prevents UI widgets from receiving keyboard or gamepad focus. Use this when the player should control the character or camera without unintended menu interactions. UIOnly routes every relevant input to the UI, disabling gameplay input — this is ideal for full-screen menus, settings, or inventory systems where mouse or controller navigation must not move the player. GameAndUI delivers input to both systems and can be useful for hybrid interfaces, but it introduces the risk that a single event triggers both a UI action and a gameplay response. For example, a click that both selects an inventory slot and fires a weapon if not consumed. A common misconception is that GameAndUI is a “safe default” — in reality it requires explicit event consumption or careful routing to avoid conflicts. Remember also to set the mouse cursor visibility when switching modes: show it for UI-only or hybrid modes and hide it when returning to GameOnly. As a quick practice, try describing which mode you’d use for an in-game map that the player must pan with the mouse while still being able to aim — that design decision reveals whether the input should be routed to game, UI, or both.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Input modes control whether gameplay, UI, or both receive input events.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › Input Modes Defined
Definition

GameOnly, UIOnly, GameAndUI

These modes are configured through SetInputMode on APlayerController. They determine whether UI widgets receive focus and whether gameplay input remains active.

FInputModeGameOnly
Route all input to gameplay systems; UI will not accept keyboard or gamepad input.
FInputModeUIOnly
Route input to UI only. Show cursor and block gameplay controls.
FInputModeGameAndUI
Allow both UI and game to receive input; manage event consumption carefully.
Concrete Example
Pause Menu

When opening a pause menu you typically pause the game, show the cursor, and switch to UIOnly so menu navigation does not move the player. When the menu closes, revert to GameOnly and hide the cursor.

Key takeaway
Key Takeaway

Pick the simplest input mode that achieves your UX goal. Use GameAndUI only when you design clear event consumption rules.

screens.title: GameOnly vs UIOnly: Practical trade-offs
screens.subtitle: When to prefer one mode over the other and common pitfalls

narration.text: Choosing between GameOnly and UIOnly affects player control and expectations. GameOnly is the safe default for uninterrupted gameplay: inputs move the player, trigger abilities, and control the camera. It’s inappropriate when the player needs to type, click widgets, or navigate menus. UIOnly is designed for those cases — it disables gameplay input and presents a cursor for direct interaction. For example, a settings screen should use UIOnly so changing toggles doesn't cause the character to react. A frequent pitfall is forgetting to hide the cursor and revert input mode when a menu closes; this can leave the player unable to control their character. Another edge case is text input inside the UI: even in GameOnly the mouse might interact with the viewport but the keyboard won’t control widgets unless you explicitly set focus or switch modes. A misconception is that UIOnly always pauses the game; it does not by itself pause time. If you need the game world frozen, also call SetGamePaused. Remember to plan the UI lifecycle: create or reuse the widget, set focus, set input mode, optionally pause, and then play any entry animation. That sequence keeps behavior consistent and predictable.

keyIdea.title: Trade-off
keyIdea.text: Use GameOnly for uninterrupted play; use UIOnly for full interaction. Pause explicitly when required.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › GameOnly vs UIOnly
GameOnly
All input goes to the game. UI widgets will not receive keyboard or gamepad input unless you explicitly set focus or switch modes.
  • Use for core gameplay and camera control.
  • Mouse may still affect viewport but widgets won’t process keyboard/gamepad events.
  • Does not pause the game automatically.
UIOnly
All input routes to UI. Show the mouse cursor and set focus to the primary widget for predictable navigation.
  • Use for menus, inventories, settings screens.
  • Remember to set bShowMouseCursor = true when opening UIOnly.
  • Call SetGamePaused(true) separately if you must freeze game time.
Pitfall
Leaving input mode unchanged when closing UI can lock controls or leave the cursor visible.
Pro tip
Encapsulate mode changes in a single toggle function to reduce state bugs.
Check
When testing, verify both mouse and gamepad navigation paths after toggling UI.

screens.title: TogglePauseMenu — Implementation Walkthrough
screens.subtitle: A concrete example using SetInputMode and SetGamePaused

narration.text: We will walk through the typical TogglePauseMenu flow used in many projects. The goal is to pause the game when the menu opens, show the cursor, create and add the widget, and return to normal input when closing. The high-level steps are: check your paused flag, call SetGamePaused with true or false, create or remove the widget, set the input mode to UIOnly or GameOnly, and set bShowMouseCursor appropriately. The provided C++ snippet demonstrates these steps in a single function, making the toggle atomic and reducing state bugs. As a concrete example, assume you press the Pause key: TogglePauseMenu will set bIsGamePaused true, call CreateWidget and AddToViewport for your PauseMenuWidgetClass, then build an FInputModeUIOnly instance and set it on the player controller. It also calls SetWidgetToFocus so the first button receives focus. A common mistake is not binding a FadeIn animation; if the widget uses a bound animation you should play it on construct. Finally, remember to remove or collapse the widget when resuming the game; using RemoveFromParent frees the widget, while setting visibility to Collapsed keeps it in memory for reuse. Which approach you pick depends on memory trade-offs and how often the menu appears.

keyIdea.title: Implementation pattern
keyIdea.text: Toggle pause: SetGamePaused ↔ Create/Add widget ↔ SetInputMode(UIOnly) ↔ Show cursor; reverse when resuming.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › TogglePauseMenu Walkthrough
Code example
// Example: Toggling a Pause Menu
void AMyPlayerController::TogglePauseMenu()
{
    if (bIsGamePaused)
    {
        // Resume game
        UGameplayStatics::SetGamePaused(GetWorld(), false);
        bIsGamePaused = false;
        if (PauseMenuWidget)
        {
            PauseMenuWidget->RemoveFromParent();
            PauseMenuWidget = nullptr;
        }
        FInputModeGameOnly InputMode;
        SetInputMode(InputMode);
        bShowMouseCursor = false;
    }
    else
    {
        // Pause game
        UGameplayStatics::SetGamePaused(GetWorld(), true);
        bIsGamePaused = true;
        if (PauseMenuWidgetClass)
        {
            PauseMenuWidget = CreateWidget<UUserWidget>(this, PauseMenuWidgetClass);
            if (PauseMenuWidget)
            {
                PauseMenuWidget->AddToViewport();
            }
        }
        FInputModeUIOnly InputMode;
        InputMode.SetWidgetToFocus(PauseMenuWidget->TakeWidget());
        InputMode.SetLockMouseToViewportBehavior(EMouseLockMode::DoNotLock);
        SetInputMode(InputMode);
        bShowMouseCursor = true;
    }
}
Explanation
  • Check the paused flag to decide branch. Toggle game pause state to freeze or resume game logic.
  • Create or remove the pause widget. AddToViewport displays it, RemoveFromParent unloads it.
  • Set input mode: UIOnly when paused, GameOnly when resuming. SetWidgetToFocus ensures controller focus.
  • Toggle bShowMouseCursor so the player can interact with widgets when needed.
Common mistake
Not clearing the PauseMenuWidget pointer after removal can cause dangling references. Always null out stored widget references when you RemoveFromParent.

screens.title: UI Focus & Navigation
screens.subtitle: Ensuring predictable gamepad and keyboard flows

narration.text: Focus and navigation determine which widget receives keyboard or gamepad events. When you open a menu, explicitly set focus to the first actionable control so a gamepad user can immediately navigate. Use Widget->SetUserFocus on the owning player controller to assign focus, or Widget->SetKeyboardFocus when keyboard text input is required. In complex layouts automatic navigation can skip items; use SetNavigationRule in the UMG Designer to declare Up, Down, Left, and Right relationships between widgets. A concrete example: a settings vertical box with Video, Audio, Controls buttons should have Down navigation from Video set to Audio so controller input never jumps over items. Misconceptions include assuming that adding widgets in a particular order guarantees navigation order — UMG’s automatic navigation can vary depending on layout, composition, and nested containers. Always test with a controller. For a robust flow: when a menu opens, set input mode, set the target widget to focus, confirm navigation rules, and then play your entry animation. That sequence ensures both accessibility and a smooth first interaction for controller users. UI Focus & Navigation means always set initial focus and explicit navigation rules for controller predictability.. In practical terms, ensuring predictable gamepad and keyboard flows. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Focus rule
keyIdea.text: Always set initial focus and explicit navigation rules for controller predictability.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › UI Focus & Navigation
Steps to reliable focus
  1. Open or show the widget and ensure the owning player controller is available.
  2. Call SetUserFocus or SetKeyboardFocus on the target widget.
  3. Set or verify explicit navigation rules in the UMG Designer when automatic behavior fails.
  4. Test with a controller and keyboard to confirm the flow is predictable.
Concrete scenario
A vertical list of menu buttons sometimes skips a button when navigating with a gamepad. Fix it by opening the widget, selecting the first button, and setting Down navigation explicitly for each button in the Designer. This ensures stable movement between items regardless of layout changes.
Misconception
Layout order always determines navigation. In practice, nested containers and padding can alter automatic rules; explicit navigation is more reliable.

screens.title: Common Advanced UI Patterns
screens.subtitle: Pause menus, inventory screens, pop-ups and loading screens

narration.text: Advanced UIs are built from recurring patterns that share similar lifecycle and input concerns. Pause menus typically pause time, switch to UIOnly, show the cursor, and accept controller navigation. Inventory screens can be UIOnly when they fully capture input, or GameAndUI when you want to allow simultaneous gameplay actions; the choice depends on whether the player should be able to move while manipulating items. Pop-up dialogs are overlay widgets which may temporarily switch input mode or rely on careful event consumption if layered above other interactive widgets. Loading screens are often full-screen widgets created early in the GameInstance and removed when loading completes. The practical design decision is to identify whether interaction must be exclusive (use UIOnly), shared (use GameAndUI with consumption), or primarily gameplay-driven (use GameOnly and set focus only for targeted text fields). For inventories, also plan for drag-and-drop: that requires visible cursor and usually UIOnly to avoid accidental character movement while dragging. These patterns also share common cleanup responsibilities: remove or hide widgets, reset input modes, and null any stored pointers to avoid leaks or dangling references.

keyIdea.title: Pattern guide
keyIdea.text: Match input mode and lifecycle to the pattern: exclusive UI for focused work, hybrid when interaction must coexist with gameplay.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › Advanced UI Patterns
Pause Menu
Pause game, UIOnly, show cursor, set focus to first button, play fade-in animation. On resume remove widget and revert input mode.
Inventory
Often UIOnly for drag-and-drop. Alternatively, use GameAndUI if you must retain some gameplay controls while UI is visible, but consume events that would otherwise trigger gameplay.
Pop-ups & Dialogs
Overlay widgets that may temporarily take focus. Decide whether the overlay should claim UIOnly or simply capture events within itself.
Loading Screens
Create early in GameInstance, show until loading ends, then remove. Use minimal animations to avoid extra draw cost during load operations.
Lifecycle: Create or Show → SetInputMode → SetFocus → Animate → Hide/Remove
Drag-and-drop requires cursor and exclusive input for predictable interaction.
Cleanup: RemoveFromParent vs Collapsed — choose based on reuse frequency and memory trade-offs.

screens.title: Widget Animation & Binding
screens.subtitle: Using UWidgetAnimation and BindWidgetAnim in C++

narration.text: Widget animations give your UI polish and feedback. In UMG you author animations that modify properties like opacity, position, or scale, and you can trigger them from Blueprint or C++. To access an animation in C++, declare a UPROPERTY marked Transient with meta BindWidgetAnim and a UWidgetAnimation* type. When your UUserWidget subclass constructs, check that the animation pointer is valid and call PlayAnimation to run it. A common pattern is to play a fade-in animation on construct so the menu appears smoothly. A misconception is trying to animate widgets by continuously modifying properties in Event Tick; using UWidgetAnimation produced by the Designer is preferred because it’s optimized and declarative. If you must drive motion procedurally, keep updates event-driven and throttle frequency. Also only bind animations in C++ when you need programmatic control; for purely visual, Blueprint triggers are sufficient. Properly binding and playing animations gives you deterministic start points and makes it easier to coordinate input mode changes and focus after the animation completes. Widget Animation & Binding means bind animations using bindwidgetanim and call playanimation safely in nativeconstruct to add polish without tick.. content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › Widget Animation & Binding
Header

Bind a UWidgetAnimation in C++

// In UMyPauseMenuWidget.h
UPROPERTY(Transient, meta=(BindWidgetAnim))
UWidgetAnimation* FadeInAnimation;

// In UMyPauseMenuWidget.cpp
void UMyPauseMenuWidget::NativeConstruct()
{
    Super::NativeConstruct();
    if (FadeInAnimation)
    {
        PlayAnimation(FadeInAnimation);
    }
}
Explanation
  • BindWidgetAnim attaches the Designer animation to a C++ pointer at runtime.
  • Call PlayAnimation in NativeConstruct to start the animation when the widget appears.
  • Avoid using Event Tick for animation; prefer Designer animations for performance and authoring clarity.
Pro tip: If an animation must complete before input is allowed, disable focus until OnAnimationFinished fires, then set focus and input mode.

screens.title: Performance Optimization for UIs
screens.subtitle: Avoiding common rendering and update pitfalls

narration.text: As UIs grow, performance becomes a first-class concern. Avoid placing frequently changing logic inside Event Tick on widgets; prefer event-driven updates so the UI reacts only when data changes. For visibility and rendering, use ESlateVisibility::Collapsed to remove a widget from layout and rendering, or Hidden to keep layout space but skip rendering — RemoveFromParent fully unloads the widget and frees resources. Reusing widgets and setting visibility is typically faster than repeatedly creating and destroying complex hierarchies in performance-sensitive contexts. Reduce draw calls by minimizing unique textures and materials; use atlases and shared fonts where possible to lower G P U cost. Break complex screens into smaller child widgets so the engine can cull or update only the parts that change. A common mistake is gratuitous nesting or creating dynamic elements every frame; this increases memory churn and draw cost. When profiling, watch for spikes caused by creating widgets at once during a pause or loading sequence; consider staggering or pre-creating assets during loading to smooth runtime performance. Performance Optimization for UIs means prefer event-driven updates, reuse widgets, minimize unique textures, and choose visibility states wisely.. keyIdea.title: Perf rules
keyIdea.text: Prefer event-driven updates, reuse widgets, minimize unique textures, and choose visibility states wisely.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › Performance Optimization
Avoid Event Tick

If you update UI each frame, you consume CPU and possibly thread contention. Instead, update widgets only when the underlying data changes, such as inventory contents or health values.

Use Collapsed or Hidden for quick toggles without reallocating widget trees.
RemoveFromParent when you need to free memory for rarely used screens.
Draw call reduction

Reduce unique textures and use atlases. Group static imagery to avoid multiple material switches.

Checklist
  • Avoid Tick where possible.
  • Reuse widgets and toggle visibility.
  • Break big widgets into children for selective updates.

screens.title: Build a Pause Menu — Step-by-step
screens.subtitle: Create WBP_PauseMenu, bind animation, and toggle from your PlayerController

narration.text: This hands-on activity walks you through creating a pause menu that toggles cleanly and plays a fade-in. Start by creating a Widget Blueprint named WBP_PauseMenu with a Canvas Panel root. Add a centered Vertical Box containing three Buttons labeled Resume, Options, and Quit. In the Animations panel create FadeInAnimation that changes the root panel’s render opacity from 0 to 1 over half a second. In your player controller add a TSubclassOf for the PauseMenuWidgetClass and a UUserWidget pointer for PauseMenuWidget along with a bIsGamePaused boolean. Implement TogglePauseMenu to pause the game, create and add the widget, set the input mode to UIOnly, set the widget to focus, and set bShowMouseCursor true. For resume, reverse the steps and remove the widget. Optionally create a MyPauseMenuWidget C++ subclass and add a Transient BindWidgetAnim property for FadeInAnimation, then call PlayAnimation in NativeConstruct. Test by binding the Pause action to TogglePauseMenu and verify the cursor appears, the game pauses, and the fade runs. This practical sequence ensures you have a repeatable, testable pause flow. screens.title: Assessment & Common Mistakes
screens.subtitle: Checks to verify correct input and navigation behavior

narration.text: To assess your implementation, use scenario-based checks that mirror real player actions. For example, open an inventory that supports click-and-drag. The inventory should block character movement and show the cursor; this demonstrates correct use of UIOnly and bShowMouseCursor. Another assessment: create a vertical options menu and navigate with a controller. If Down sometimes skips items, set explicit navigation rules and verify that SetUserFocus is called on open. Also test hybrid behavior: design a small map overlay that should allow panning with the mouse while aiming remains active; if both are active without event consumption you may trigger unintended actions — this shows the risks of using GameAndUI without consumption. Common mistakes include leaving widgets in memory unintentionally, not nulling references after RemoveFromParent, and leaving Event Tick active in UMG. For a thorough test, create a checklist: toggle the menu repeatedly, test with mouse and controller, validate focus landing, and profile draw and tick overhead. Each failed check points to a targeted fix rather than guessing where the bug lives. content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › Assessment & Mistakes
Assessment checks
  • Inventory open: UIOnly active, cursor visible, drag-and-drop functions and no character movement.
  • Pause toggle: game paused, fade-in plays, and Resume returns to GameOnly with cursor hidden.
  • Controller navigation: first button receives focus and Down navigation goes to next item reliably.
Common mistakes
  • Not resetting input mode and cursor when closing menus.
  • Leaving pointers to removed widgets, causing dangling references.
  • Using Tick for UI updates rather than event-driven updates.
Quick fix: centralize toggle behavior in one function on the PlayerController to avoid duplicated mode changes across Blueprints or widgets.

screens.title: Designing Reusable UI Components
screens.subtitle: Modularity, child widgets, and memory-aware design

narration.text: Large UIs benefit from modularity. Break screens into smaller child widgets for distinct responsibilities: a header widget, an item slot widget, and a pager or scrollbar widget. This makes logic easier to test and reduces work when only a subset needs updating. For inventory lists, create a reusable ItemSlot widget and populate it dynamically; when content changes, refresh only slots affected by the change. Memory-wise, choose between RemoveFromParent and visibility states: RemoveFromParent frees memory but requires recreation, which can be costly if toggled frequently. Collapsed is a useful compromise for short-lived UIs as it removes rendering and layout cost while keeping allocation. For animations, bind only the animations you need in C++ and keep specialized behaviors contained in the child widgets. Finally, centralize input-mode toggles at the PlayerController to avoid conflicts when multiple widgets request different modes. This reduces race conditions and ensures a single source of truth for input routing in your game. Designing Reusable UI Components means use child widgets, reusable slot components, and centralized input control to reduce bugs and improve performance.. In practical terms, modularity, child widgets, and memory-aware design. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Modularity
keyIdea.text: Use child widgets, reusable slot components, and centralized input control to reduce bugs and improve performance.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › Reusable UI Components
Component strategy
  • Create small child widgets for repeating elements.
  • Populate lists dynamically and update only changed items.
  • Localize animations and logic to children to reduce coupling.
Memory pattern
Use Collapsed for quick hides, Hidden if you need layout preservation, and RemoveFromParent when you want to free resources permanently. Pre-create rarely changing elements during loading to avoid spikes.
Centralize SetInputMode in PlayerController so widgets request changes through a single API. This prevents conflicting mode changes when multiple widgets are active.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: What to remember from Advanced UI & Input Handling

narration.text: These three compact concepts should stay top of mind. First, input modes — GameOnly, UIOnly, and GameAndUI — define where events are routed and require explicit cursor changes and sometimes pausing. Second, focus and navigation must be explicitly managed for controller and keyboard users; set initial focus and use navigation rules to avoid unpredictable jumps. Third, widget animation and performance go hand in hand: bind and play Designer animations for polish, and prefer event-driven updates over Tick. Together these concepts form a practical checklist you can apply when building a pause menu, inventory, or dialog system in your game. Before moving on, ask yourself: can you toggle all required state from a single PlayerController function and verify behavior with both mouse and gamepad? If yes, you have a robust UI toggle flow.

Summary

Correct input routing, predictable focus, and efficient animations together form the foundation of robust, accessible game UIs.

narration.text: End with three quick reminders you can apply immediately. First, always pair input mode changes with cursor visibility toggles; forgetting bShowMouseCursor is a frequent usability bug. Second, centralize input-mode state in the PlayerController to avoid conflicting requests from multiple widgets. Third, prefer visibility toggles and widget reuse over repeated creation and destruction when you expect frequent shows and hides. These rules reduce bugs, make testing easier, and improve runtime performance. Before you implement, sketch the lifecycle for any UI: when it is created, how input is routed while visible, what animation should run, and how it is cleaned up.
